The way it's "normally" done, and has been for 20+ years that I've been involved with computer security issues. The ones who find the backdoor work with the vendor, or at least give the vendor the proof of concept code and a head-start to fix the problem. This is the civilised way, works fine as long as the vendor/maintainer has the will to keep the product in good order, only really fails when the vendor wants to do a cover-up instead of a fix. Sometimes the vendor is mere months away from a new version of their code, and doesn't want to waste resources fixing the old version, which causes a conflict between the security guy and the vendor.

If the vendor won't cooperate or is too slow the researchers go public with a "proof of concept exploit" which is normally enough code that another programmer familiar with what's suppsed to be wrong can see if it's true or not. This is called full disclosure. Normally the proof of concept exploit is crippled so that it doesn't get used by every wannabe skript kiddie that can run a compiler.

Sometimes a rogue researcher will go straight to step 2, publish the code. Some researchers actually believe this is a better way to handle security bugs. Can't say I agree, and it's against management policy at my workplace, but I've heard the arguments from both sides and they both have good points.
